\chapter{Research and Existing Solutions}
\section{Research Method / Approach}\label{ch2:sec:method}
The research behind FlakeTrace used five sources of evidence. Each one is recorded in the
project's documentation folder, so every claim in this chapter can be traced back to it.

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Literature review.} 41 sources on flaky and order-dependent tests, minimisation,
  repair, statistics and benchmark reproducibility are listed in
  \nolinkurl{docs/01-Literature/references.md}. Each of the closest research systems has its
  own note recording what it does, what it leaves open and how FlakeTrace relates to it. A
  separate note lists what we must never claim as our own, for example delta-debugging
  minimisation and the polluter/victim vocabulary.
\item \textbf{Product review.} The published documentation of three commercial flaky-test
  products (Trunk Flaky Tests, Tuist and Gradle Develocity) was compared on the same questions
  (\nolinkurl{docs/01-Literature/commercial-tools.md}).
\item \textbf{Previous FYPs.} All 989 project records in the department's FYP repository from
  Fall 2019 to Fall 2025 were searched for testing, flakiness, test-order, CI and debugging
  terms, and the full record of every hit was read. Three projects were structurally comparable;
  none deals with order dependence (\nolinkurl{docs/01-Literature/prior-fyp-comparison.md}).
\item \textbf{Practitioner interviews.} Three developers from three companies answered 14
  questions in 15--20 minutes each, about process and timing only; no source code or customer
  data was collected (\nolinkurl{docs/00-Meta/stakeholder-evidence.md}). All three described the
  same manual procedure for an order-dependent failure: rerun the failing test after smaller and
  smaller groups of earlier tests until the culprit appears. None had a tool for it. Their
  projects use Python, JavaScript and TypeScript, not Java, so the interviews support the shape
  of the problem, not the claim that Java teams in particular have it.
\item \textbf{Proof of concept (POC).} From 25 to 28 August 2026 the team tested the proposal's
  central assumption before building anything (\nolinkurl{docs/05-Testing/poc/poc-log.md}).
  The definitions and pass/fail gates were committed before any experiment ran. Cases came from
  the Illinois Dataset of Flaky Tests \cite{idoft}: its 8,075 rows were filtered to 1,438
  order-dependent rows, and then to 8 targets in two Java projects (json-iterator and fastjson)
  built at fixed commits. The runs used clean JDK~8 containers with the network switched off.
  Four targets, all in fastjson, reproduced; 2,606 test orders were executed in total. The
  result is discussed in Section~\ref{ch2:sec:challenges}.
\end{enumerate}
\section{Existing Solutions / Products}\label{ch2:sec:existing}
Six research systems, three commercial products and three earlier FYPs are close to FlakeTrace.
For each one, this section states what its publication or documentation describes, using the
team's notes in \nolinkurl{docs/01-Literature/per-paper/}.

\paragraph{Detection: iDFlakies.} iDFlakies \cite{lam2019idflakies} is a Maven plugin for JUnit
projects that detects flaky tests by rerunning them, both in the original order and in random or
reversed orders, and then partly classifies each one as order-dependent or not. Its dataset of 422
flaky tests is 50.5\% order-dependent. It also sets two rules for valid shuffled orders: methods of
different test classes are never mixed, because JUnit never runs them that way, and classes are
shuffled before the methods inside each class. It does not say which earlier test causes a
failure.

\paragraph{Polluter search and repair: iFixFlakies.} iFixFlakies \cite{shi2019ifixflakies}
introduced the vocabulary this report uses: a \emph{victim} passes alone but fails after a
\emph{polluter}; a \emph{brittle} test fails alone and needs a \emph{state-setter} to run first; a
\emph{cleaner} run in between undoes the pollution. A test's type is decided by running it alone.
Its Minimizer applies delta debugging \cite{zeller2002ddmin} to the tests that ran before the
order-dependent test to find its polluters or state-setters, and its Patcher builds a fix from the
code of existing helper tests: cleaners for victims, state-setters for brittle tests. The result of delta debugging is 1-minimal: removing any single test
stops the failure, but a smaller set may exist.

\paragraph{Ranking: RankF.} RankF \cite{rahman2025rankf} orders the candidate tests so that a
responsible one is confirmed sooner. RankFL learns from the test code; RankFO scores candidates
from the outcomes of previously observed test orders. On 155 order-dependent tests from 24 projects
it found the first responsible test in a median of 9.4--14.1\,s, against 34.2--118.5\,s for the
baselines. It leaves out failures that need several tests together, and RankFO needs earlier test
orders to learn from.

\paragraph{Explanation: Takuan.} Takuan \cite{levin2025takuan} compares dynamic invariants recorded
during a passing order with those from a failing order. An invariant that holds only in the
passing order can show the ``clean'' value of the shared state. It can also search for methods
that reset that state, and it handles external state such as files. Its evaluation is explicitly
preliminary: 13 tests, with correct invariants produced for 6.

\paragraph{State-pollution detection: PolDet and ElectricTest.} PolDet \cite{gyori2015poldet}
compares the shared heap and the file system before a test's setup and after its teardown, and
reports an access path or a file name as evidence. On 26 projects and 6,105 tests it reported 324
polluting tests, of which manual inspection judged 194 to be relevant. ElectricTest
\cite{bell2015electrictest} monitors test execution and reports the code, with a stack trace, that
creates a dependency between tests; detecting dependencies soundly slowed execution by about 20
times on average.

\paragraph{Repair: ODRepair and FlakyDoctor.} When no cleaner exists, ODRepair
\cite{li2022odrepair} generates the cleaning code instead. FlakyDoctor \cite{chen2024flakydoctor}
combines a language model with program analysis and repaired 57\% of 332 order-dependent tests.
Both start from an order-dependent test whose polluter is already known: they work after
diagnosis, not instead of it.

\paragraph{Commercial products.} Trunk Flaky Tests, Tuist and Gradle Develocity detect, track,
retry and quarantine flaky tests. None of the product documentation we reviewed describes
returning a verified, replayable order together with a resource-level explanation for one
order-dependent failure. We claim only that their published documentation does not describe
this, not that the products cannot do it.

\paragraph{Previous FYPs.} Three earlier FAST projects are structurally comparable.
F22-032-D-ETesting generates exploratory tests; F22-033-D-WebSPLAT reuses functional tests across
variants of a web product line; S25-049-D-TestML uses machine learning for test generation,
optimisation and defect prediction. All three create or reuse tests, while FlakeTrace diagnoses an
interaction between tests inside an existing suite. This check covers the repository summaries
only; it cannot rule out an internal module of another project.

\section{Limitations and Gaps}\label{ch2:sec:gaps}
Each part of diagnosing an order-dependent failure has already been solved by someone. Reducing a
failing order is solved by delta debugging \cite{zeller2002ddmin} as used in iFixFlakies
\cite{shi2019ifixflakies}. Ranking the likely responsible tests is solved for single polluters by
RankF \cite{rahman2025rankf}. Explaining the shared state has been shown at a preliminary scale by
Takuan \cite{levin2025takuan} and PolDet \cite{gyori2015poldet}. FlakeTrace claims none of these
techniques, nor the victim and polluter vocabulary, as its own.

The limits the papers themselves report are what leave room for this project:
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{iFixFlakies} returns a reduced order without saying how reliably it reproduces the
  failure or which shared state connects the tests, and, as the authors of ODRepair point out \cite{li2022odrepair}, its repair depends on a
  cleaner test already existing.
\item \textbf{RankF} leaves out failures that need several earlier tests together, and its
  history-based variant needs previously observed test orders.
\item \textbf{Takuan}'s evaluation covers 13 tests.
\item \textbf{Shared state alone is not proof.} PolDet reported 324 polluting tests, but manual
  inspection judged only 194 of them relevant \cite{gyori2015poldet}. A tool that blames a test
  only because it touches the same state as the victim will often be wrong.
\item \textbf{Watching execution is costly and can change the result.} ElectricTest's sound
  detection slowed execution by about 20 times \cite{bell2015electrictest}, and Luo et al.
  found that 85\% of their asynchronous-wait flaky failures appeared when a single time delay was
  added \cite{luo2014empirical}. Instrumentation heavy enough to change timing can therefore
  change the failure it is meant to explain.
\end{itemize}

\paragraph{The gap.} No system reviewed here produces a single result for one order-dependent
failure that does all of the following:
\begin{enumerate}
\item names the responsible test or tests through controlled reruns, not through state overlap
  alone;
\item states how reliably the reduced order reproduces the failure, with a statistical interval;
\item links polluter, shared resource and victim to exact code locations;
\item says clearly, with a typed reason, when the evidence does not support a conclusion;
\item spends no more than a declared execution budget.
\end{enumerate}
Iteration~1 of FlakeTrace covers points 1--4; the execution budget (point 5) is planned for a later iteration
(Section~\ref{ch2:sec:proposed}). For commercial tools the gap is narrower: their published
documentation describes detecting and quarantining flaky tests, not diagnosing a single
failure in this way.
\section{Proposed Solution}\label{ch2:sec:proposed}
FlakeTrace combines established techniques into one workflow that ends either in a result anyone
can check or in a clearly stated refusal. Given a Maven project and one failing test, it:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{reproduces} the failure in the given or discovered order, and if that fails, in up
  to 31 valid shuffled orders, and records the failure's signature;
\item \textbf{runs the victim alone}, so that a test which fails by itself is never blamed on
  another test;
\item \textbf{finds the polluter or polluters}, first one at a time and, when no single test is
  enough, by delta debugging to a 1-minimal set;
\item \textbf{repeats} the reduced order 20 times and gives a 95\% Wilson interval for how often
  it reproduces the failure;
\item \textbf{names the shared resource} and the exact bytecode locations where the polluter
  writes it and the victim reads it, from the compiled classes, without running or changing the
  code;
\item \textbf{decides} \texttt{VERIFIED}, \texttt{CANDIDATE}, or \texttt{UNRESOLVED} with a
  typed reason.
\end{enumerate}
The project's files are hashed before and after every diagnosis to show that nothing was changed.
Chapter~5 gives the design.

Iteration~1 runs this whole path from one command on the team's fixture project. Fixture cases
F1--F4 are \texttt{VERIFIED}: each failure reproduced 20 times out of 20 and never alone. N1 and
N2 are \texttt{UNRESOLVED} because the victim fails alone, and N3 is \texttt{UNRESOLVED} because
the failure never reproduced, not even in 31 shuffled orders (Table~\ref{ch8:tab:fixture-results}).
These are the cases the design was built to handle; they do not yet show how the tool performs
on real projects.

This answers the first four points of the gap in Section~\ref{ch2:sec:gaps}: the culprit is found
by controlled reruns, the reproduction rate comes with an interval, the evidence names exact code
locations, and an inconclusive case gets a typed reason instead of a guess. The remaining parts of
the approved scope are not built yet and are planned for later iterations (Section~\ref{ch1:sec:scope}):
\begin{itemize}
\item an explicit execution budget and the ranking of candidate tests before the search;
\item filesystem paths as a third resource family;
\item running diagnoses inside a locked-down container;
\item runtime evidence, kept as a fallback for cases static analysis cannot explain (ADR-001);
\item evaluation against published baselines, including iFixFlakies and RankF, on a frozen
  benchmark of real projects.
\end{itemize}
\section{Complex Computing Problem}\label{ch2:sec:ccp}
The problem FlakeTrace addresses is stated in one sentence in the team's project summary:
\begin{quote}
Allocating a finite execution budget across competing diagnostic actions under uncertainty, and
knowing when the evidence does not justify a claim.
\end{quote}
In full, the tool must produce evidence that can be reproduced on another machine, is minimal under
a declared rule, is supported by an observed shared-resource interaction and comes with a
statistical measure of reliability. At the same time the search is bounded, the analysis must not
change the behaviour it studies, and the tool must refuse to answer rather than answer wrongly.
These are not separate requirements that can be met one after another: each one limits the others.

The team claims seven of the nine Seoul Accord characteristics of a complex computing problem.
Table~\ref{ch2:tab:ccp} gives the evidence for each and states how much of it Iteration~1 already
shows; parts that depend on the execution budget are planned for later iterations.

The conflict between depth of analysis and its cost has already been measured. On the fastjson
case FJ-01, static analysis at depths 1--3 found none of the 42 tests that really affect the
victim; at depth~4 it found all 42, plus one false edge among the 30 tests that do not. That false
edge comes from a test that writes the shared time-zone field but restores it afterwards, which the
static analysis does not model. One pair took about 3--6~s to analyse at depth~2, but 7.5~s for
FJ-01 at depth~4 and 26.3~s for FJ-02 at depth~5 (ADR-006). FlakeTrace therefore starts at depth~2
and goes deeper only when no edge is found.

Two characteristics are not claimed. \textbf{Diverse stakeholders} would hold only if interviews
showed that developers, QA engineers and CI maintainers need materially different things, and that
those differences shape the requirements. The three practitioner interviews done so far (a chief
executive, an engineering lead and a full-stack engineer) describe overlapping needs rather than
conflicting ones. \textbf{Unfamiliar issues} is not claimed because
using an unfamiliar framework does not count; the team has not yet set out which new computing
knowledge the problem itself demands.
\section{Technical Challenges}\label{ch2:sec:challenges}
This section describes the main technical challenges met so far, in the proof of concept and in
Iteration~1, and how each was handled. Open challenges are listed at the end.

\paragraph{Running tests in an exact order without touching the project.} Every experiment depends
on running a chosen list of tests in exactly that order, each list in a fresh JVM, with every test
reported, a crash counted as a failure, and nothing added to or written into the analysed
project. It also has to work on Windows, WSL and the Ubuntu CI runners with JDK~8. The order
runner starts a small Java harness for each run that calls JUnit's own \texttt{JUnitCore} on one
test method at a time and writes the results to a file, so that a test printing to the console
cannot corrupt them (ADR-003). The project's files are hashed before and after every diagnosis;
a mismatch ends the diagnosis as \texttt{UNRESOLVED}.

\paragraph{The test harness can create or hide the failure.} The proof of concept showed this
twice. On jsoniter, running test methods without the suite classes that the project's build
normally uses made 182 of 210 candidate tests ``fail'' with the same \texttt{LinkageError}; once
the suite context was reproduced, the count fell to zero. On fastjson, an earlier version of the
harness set the time zone to make two failing tests pass alone, which erased the very dependence
being measured. Both were found and corrected. The lesson carried into the design is that the tool
must show it did not cause a result before it reports one, and that a test which fails alone is a
finding to classify, not an environment problem to fix.

\paragraph{Failures that need more than one polluter.} Trying each earlier test on its own finds a
single polluter, but fixture case F3 fails only when two tests have both run before the victim. On
F3, the one-by-one search ends with no single polluter after 12 runs. FlakeTrace then runs delta
debugging \cite{zeller2002ddmin} over the earlier tests (ADR-007). Delta debugging returns a
\emph{1-minimal} set, one from which no single test can be removed, and may miss other
combinations, so the report never calls the result ``minimum''.

\paragraph{Failures that do not reproduce.} The order FlakeTrace discovers may not be the order
the CI server ran, so repeating it can never show a failure that needs another order. FlakeTrace
therefore tries up to 31 valid shuffled orders before it gives up (ADR-008). If none reproduces
the failure, the result is \texttt{UNRESOLVED} with the reason \texttt{NOT\_REPRODUCED} and a
record of what was tried. It never says the test is reliable, because no number of reruns can
prove that.

\paragraph{Finding the shared resource from compiled code.} At the depths first agreed (1--3),
static analysis explained none of the real fastjson cases, because the victims reach the shared
field only inside constructors four or five calls deep. A fixed depth of 5 would make every pair
pay the highest cost and the most over-approximation. FlakeTrace starts at depth~2 and deepens one
level at a time, up to 5, only when no edge has been found and the depth limit was hit (ADR-006).
One known false edge remains: a test that changes the shared field but restores it afterwards,
because the analysis does not model the values written (Section~\ref{ch2:sec:ccp}).

\paragraph{Static analysis or a runtime agent.} At the proposal defence the panel asked whether
trace code would be injected and whether the analysed code would be modified. The team's
post-defence plan named a runtime Java agent as the preferred way to observe shared state, while the team's report contract fixes the evidence level at
static-only for Iteration~1. ADR-001 resolved this: Iteration~1 uses controlled reruns and static
bytecode analysis with no instrumentation, and a runtime agent is kept as the Iteration~2 fallback for
cases static analysis cannot explain.

\paragraph{Open challenges.}
\begin{itemize}
\item The overhead of runtime evidence collection has no measured value yet; it will be measured
  before any threshold is set.
\item FlakeTrace's own code has so far been run on one real project, fastjson, which relies
  heavily on global static configuration and is therefore favourable to static analysis.
\item The published baseline tools, including iFixFlakies and RankF, have not been run yet; only
  the team's own baseline has been run, on fixture cases F1--F4.
\end{itemize}

The proof of concept also changed the design directly (Section~\ref{ch2:sec:challenges}). Its
null result at depth~1 led to a configurable analysis depth starting at~2. Its time-zone mistake
led to the rule that a test failing alone is classified, never ``fixed'' by changing the
environment. Its fake polluters led to the rule that the runner must reproduce the project's own
execution context.

Two questions remain open for later iterations. Evaluation will use the metrics RankF reports, such as the
rank of the first true polluter, so that results can be compared directly with it
\cite{rahman2025rankf}. No paper reviewed gives a ratio for splitting a fixed budget between
searching and verifying, so the split is project policy, and running without a verification
reserve will be tested as an ablation.
